== Specification/basic/inference.tex:47-280

\section{The Static Arguments of a Call}
\seclabel{static-arg-inference}

The static arguments of a call that does not write them are found in two
steps: the declaration that the call invokes is chosen first, and it is
instantiated second.

\emph{Choice.}
The declaration is chosen as \secref{resolving-coercion} describes.
A declaration with static parameters is applicable to a call, without or with
coercion, if some instance of it whose static arguments satisfy their bounds is
applicable to the call.
Declarations are compared on the parameter types they declare, a declaration
with static parameters on its parameter types taken over every instance that
its bounds allow, and not on an instance inferred for the call.
So a coercion is applied only to make a call possible: it never changes which
declaration is chosen when one is applicable to the call without it.

\emph{Instantiation.}
The static arguments of the chosen declaration are then inferred, and with them
the instance of the declaration that the call invokes:
\begin{itemize}
\item A type parameter, or a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter, that the
declared type of a parameter mentions other than as the whole type, as
\EXP{b\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket} mentions \VAR{T}, is fixed by
the argument at that position, whose type must be a subtype of the parameter
type of the instance.
\item Where the call has an expected type (below), a type parameter that the
declared return type mentions other than as the whole type is fixed by the
expected type as well.
\item A type parameter that is the whole declared type of one or more
parameters, as \VAR{T} is of \EXP{x\COLON{}T}, and that is not fixed as above,
takes, among the types of the arguments at those positions and the types to
which they can be coerced, the narrowest under $\morespecificeq$
(\secref{resolving-coercion}) that every one of those arguments is
substitutable for (\secref{applicability-with-coercion}) and that the bounds of
the type parameter permit.
For number arguments this is the narrowest type into which every one of them
converts: \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, and also for a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and an
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32}, though neither of them is a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}
(\secref{basic-integers}).
Where there is no such narrowest type, and the rule for numerals
(\secref{numeral-default}) does not settle the tie, the type parameter takes
the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has
none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type (below), where the call
has one, requires of the declared return type, provided the types of those
arguments are subtypes of it; none of those arguments is converted.
\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 gave such
a type parameter the union of the types of those arguments; on 29~September 2026
the revival took the rule by which the dispatcher of the type group's paper of
2019 instantiates a type parameter, which gives the bound.}
\item A type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes as
above, such as a type parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole
type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper bounds: its declared bound,
\TYP{Any} if it has none (\secref{type-param}), and what the expected type
(below), where the call has one, requires of the declared return type.
Inference never instantiates a static parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, which
programmers must not write (\secref{bottom-type}).
So, for the declaration
\EXP{\VAR{stop}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(s\COLON\TYP{String})\COLON{}T}, the
variable declaration
\EXP{x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32 = \VAR{stop}(\hbox{\rm``\STR{no}''})} instantiates
\VAR{stop} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and the same call with no expected type
instantiates it at \TYP{Any}.
\revision{revival-inference}{The revival's text of 28~September 2026 did not
describe such a type parameter and left open whether inference may give it
\TYP{BottomType}, which the team's draft note at the end of this chapter asks.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that the rule by which the dispatcher of
the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments
do not fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, which never instantiates a
type parameter at \TYP{BottomType}, is the rule of static inference as well.}
\item Every argument is then admitted against the corresponding parameter type
of the instance by substitutability: an argument whose type is a subtype of it
is passed as it is, and any other argument is coerced to it
(\secref{coercion}), as an argument is coerced to the declared type of a
parameter of a declaration without static parameters.
\end{itemize}
The coercions that the instance needs are inserted into the call statically,
as is any coercion that \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses.

\emph{The expected type.}
A call has an expected type in these contexts: as the right-hand side of a
variable or field declaration that declares its type, that type; as the
right-hand side of an assignment to a variable whose type is declared, that
type; as the body of a functional that declares its return type, that type;
as the last expression of a block that has an expected type, whether or not
local declarations precede it in the block, the block's expected type; as a
branch of an \KWD{if} expression with an \KWD{else} clause that has an
expected type, the expected type of the \KWD{if} expression; as a clause of an
\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, \TYP{()}, the type that
every such clause must have (\secref{if-expr}); as a clause of a
\KWD{typecase} expression that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause
among them, the expected type of the \KWD{typecase} expression, of which the
union of the types of its clauses, the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression
(\secref{typecase}), is then a subtype where the type of each clause is;
as the body of a \KWD{label} expression that has an expected type, or as the
\KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that
\KWD{label} expression, the expected type of the \KWD{label} expression, of
which the union of the type of its body and the types of those \KWD{with}
clause values, the type of the \KWD{label} expression (\secref{label-expr}),
is then a subtype where each of those types is; and as an argument of a call
that this section does not accept with its arguments typed without an expected
type, where the argument is itself a call with inferred static arguments, the
parameter type at the argument's position of each declaration
of the enclosing call in turn, instantiated, where that declaration has static
parameters, by the arguments that are not so typed and by the expected type of
the enclosing call alone, as described below.
The expected type is used whether the call is written by tight juxtaposition,
as \EXP{f(x)} (\secref{juxtameaning}), or by loose juxtaposition, as
\EXP{f\;x}, or as a method invocation or an operator application.
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
gave the last expression of a block an expected type only where no local
declaration precedes it, and gave none to a clause of an \KWD{if} expression
without an \KWD{else} clause, to a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression or to
a call written by loose juxtaposition; the revival decided on 8~October 2026
that each has the type that the text already requires of it.
Its text of 8~October 2026 gave none to the body of a \KWD{label} expression
or to the \KWD{with} clause expression of an \KWD{exit} expression; the
revival decided on 9~October 2026 that they have the expected type of the
\KWD{label} expression, as a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression has that of
the \KWD{typecase} expression.
Its text of 9~October 2026 gave none to an argument of another call; the
revival decided on 9~October 2026 that an argument that is itself a call with
inferred static arguments has the parameter type of each declaration
of the enclosing call in turn where the enclosing call is not accepted without
it, since the static arguments of a call ``are statically inferred from the
context of the function call'' (\secref{idn-ref}).}
The return type of the instance that the steps above find must be a subtype of
the expected type.
If they find no such instance, the static arguments are inferred again without
the expected type, and the call is accepted only if the return type of the instance
then found is a subtype of the expected type or can be coerced to it; in the
second case the result of the call is coerced to the expected type
(\secref{coercion}).
So, for the declarations
\EXP{\VAR{wrap}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}
and \EXP{\VAR{id}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(x\COLON{}T)\COLON{}T},
the variable declaration \EXP{a\COLON\TYP{List}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket = \VAR{wrap}(3)}
instantiates \VAR{wrap} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the expected type fixes,
and coerces the numeral, while \EXP{b\COLON\mathbb{Z}64 = \VAR{id}(3)}
instantiates \VAR{id} at the numeral's own type (\secref{literals}) and coerces
the result.

The arguments of a call are typed first without an expected type.
Where this section then accepts no instance of the call, each argument that is
itself a call with inferred static arguments is typed again, once
for each declaration of the enclosing call, with the parameter type at its
position as its expected type, as the list of contexts above says.
Of the declarations that are applicable to the enclosing call with its
arguments so typed, each declaration with its own, and whose instances have
return types that are subtypes of the expected type of the enclosing call,
where it has one, or can be coerced to it, the enclosing call invokes the one
that is more specific than every other on the parameter types they declare;
where there is no such declaration, the call is typed with its arguments typed
without an expected type, and is accepted or refused as above.
So where this section accepts an instance of a call with its arguments typed
without an expected type, no argument is typed again, and the declaration it
invokes is never passed over for one that only an argument typed again makes
applicable; a declaration that is applicable to those arguments but whose
return type neither is a subtype of the expected type nor can be coerced to it
is not accepted, and another may then be chosen.
For example, for the declarations
\EXP{\VAR{mk}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket()\COLON\TYP{Box}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket},
\EXP{\VAR{takes}(b\COLON\TYP{Box}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket)},
\EXP{\VAR{over}(b\COLON\TYP{Box}\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket)} and
\EXP{\VAR{over}(x\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call \EXP{\VAR{takes}(\VAR{mk}())}
instantiates \VAR{mk} at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, which the parameter type of
\VAR{takes} fixes, while the call \EXP{\VAR{over}(\VAR{mk}())} invokes the
second declaration of \VAR{over}, which is applicable to \EXP{\VAR{mk}()} typed
without an expected type, the instance of \VAR{mk} at the bound of its type
parameter.
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 9~October 2026 had
no such paragraph; the revival added it with the argument of a call to the list
of contexts above, following its decision of 9~October 2026.}

\emph{Dispatch.}
The call, with the coercions of its instance inserted, dispatches at run time
as \secref{resolving-overloading} describes, by subtyping and without further
coercion, to the most specific declaration applicable to the converted values.

For example, of the declarations
\EXP{\VAR{op}\llbracket{}T \KWD{extends} \TYP{Number}\rrbracket(a\COLON{}T, b\COLON{}T)}
and \EXP{\VAR{op}(a\COLON\TYP{Any}, b\COLON\TYP{Any})}, the call
\EXP{\VAR{op}(z, w)}, where \VAR{z} has type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \VAR{w} has
type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, chooses the first, which is applicable without
coercion, since its instance at \TYP{Number} is, and is more specific than the
second; the first is instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \VAR{z} is coerced,
and the converted call runs that instance.
\revision{revival-inference}{The interpreter has no static types and applies
the same rule at dispatch, from the run-time types of the arguments: it infers
the static arguments of a declaration with static parameters with coercion,
and instantiates the declaration that its dispatch chooses by the rule for a
type parameter that is a parameter's whole type.
So where the declared type of a variable is wider than the type of its value,
or an argument's static type is \TYP{Any}, it may run a declaration at a
narrower instance than the compiled path, which instantiates it at the static
types.
Where neither an argument's type nor a type into which the arguments convert is
the narrowest, it gives a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters
its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, as this chapter does: for a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, \TYP{Number} where that is the
bound and \TYP{Any} where the type parameter is declared without an
\KWD{extends} clause.
It does the same where the arguments that fix a type parameter inside other

Neither holds of a type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter,
itself or another, or that is declared with several bounds that the interpreter
cannot meet, as it cannot meet two bounds neither of which is a subtype of the

supertype of the arguments' run-time types that the bounds permit, where there
is one, and where there is none a call that fixes a type parameter of the
second kind fails (row~591 of the revival's gap ledger).
When its dispatch chooses among declarations, it passes over a declaration with

(row~589 of the revival's gap ledger).
It does not yet fix a type parameter by the expected type.
A type parameter that an argument bounds only from above, as a function
argument bounds the type parameter of its parameter type, it instantiates at the
intersection of the upper bounds that its declared bound and the arguments
place on it: at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} for a function of a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} where
the type parameter is declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, and at
\TYP{Number} for a function of an \TYP{Any} where it is bounded by
\TYP{Number}; such a type parameter whose bound mentions a
static parameter, or that is declared with several bounds that it cannot meet,

such a type parameter two upper bounds that it cannot meet, as a function over

== Specification/basic/inference.tex:282-402

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

This chapter does not yet describe:
\begin{itemize}
\item the static arguments of a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator
parameter (\secref{boolparams}, \secref{dimunitparams}, \secref{opr-ident});
\item a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that neither an argument nor the
expected type fixes;
\item the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine
(\secref{reduction-expr}): the rule above gives a static parameter of the big
operator that nothing at the call fixes its bounds, not the type of the
elements;
\item whether an argument whose declared parameter type mentions a static
parameter inside another type may be converted where only a conversion of its
elements would satisfy the bounds of the parameter; under the rule above such
an argument fixes the parameter by subtyping and is not converted;
\item an expected type in any context other than those listed above, such as
the body of a \KWD{for} loop;
\item the static arguments of an object with static parameters that is named
without a call, which a program writes (\secref{where-clauses});
\item the inference over a whole program of the types that declarations elide
(\secref{type-inference-components}).
\end{itemize}
\revision{revival-expected-contexts}{The revival's text of 29~September 2026
named here also an expression that a local declaration precedes in a block, an
\KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause, a \KWD{typecase} expression
and a call written by loose juxtaposition, its text of 8~October 2026 also
the body of a \KWD{label} expression, and its text of 9~October 2026 also an
argument of another call, to which the list of contexts in
\secref{static-arg-inference} now gives an expected type where the argument is
itself a call with inferred static arguments and the enclosing call
is not accepted without it.}
\revision{revival-inference}{The compiled type checker instantiates a type
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes at the
intersection of its upper bounds, as \secref{static-arg-inference} says; on the
compiled path a type parameter of a program's own declaration that is declared
without an \KWD{extends} clause is bounded by \TYP{Object} (row~412 of the
revival's gap ledger), so that a call that fixes such a parameter by nothing
else, where the expected type is one that \TYP{Object} excludes, such as
\TYP{()}, is a static error there.
A reduction's big operator is an argument of the call that the reduction's
desugaring makes, so it has an expected type only as such an argument has one:
the compiled type checker instantiates a generic big operator whose static
argument the reduction does not write at its bound, and at the reduction's
expected type only where the reduction's type at that bound does not fit it,
and it refuses the reduction where the big operator has no instance at its
bound, as one whose bound mentions its own static parameter has none (row~425
of the revival's gap ledger).
The interpreter instantiates a type parameter of a function that nothing at a
call fixes at its bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and one whose bound mentions
other static parameters at that bound with their instances, with two
exceptions: a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions, as \EXP{A \KWD{extends} T} mentions \VAR{T}, it
instantiates at the arguments' type, not at its bound, since it has no expected
type to fix it (row~592 of the revival's gap ledger); and a type parameter
declared with several bounds that it cannot meet, as two bounds neither of which
is a subtype of the other, it erases to \TYP{BottomType} (row~591).
A type parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself, as the big
operators $\sum$ and $\prod$ declare theirs, and that nothing at a call fixes,
it leaves open: it does not instantiate it, and it admits every value where it
checks a value against that type, as an argument, a variable declared with that
type, a \KWD{typecase} clause or a type assertion.
So a reduction whose element type nothing at the call fixes runs on the types
of its elements, the interpreter's counterpart of the desugaring by the type
\VAR{N} of the expression (\secref{reduction-expr}); but an empty such
reduction takes the identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the
expression (row~645 of the revival's gap ledger), and the library's set
reductions \EXP{\bigcup} and \EXP{\bigcap}, whose reductions take sets of
that open type, stop at their first element (row~662).
It still erases to \TYP{BottomType} the other static parameters of a big
operator that a reduction or a comprehension invokes without its static
arguments, a comprehension's collection being then built at the type of its
elements (row~424 of the revival's gap ledger); it gives a function expression
that declares no return type the return type \TYP{BottomType}, so that a type
parameter that only its result fixes is instantiated there (row~587); and it
leaves a generic method's static parameters uninstantiated (row~21).
The third item of the team's draft note below asks whether inference may give a
static parameter \TYP{BottomType}; the rule of \secref{static-arg-inference},
taken from the type group's paper of 2019, answers that it may not.
Neither implementation infers a \KWD{bool} parameter yet: the compiled type
checker refuses by name to infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit}
parameter, and the interpreter does not unify a \KWD{bool} one (rows~21
and~307 of the revival's gap ledger).
The example of \secref{boolparams}, a coercion whose \KWD{bool} parameter only
its parameter type mentions, can be applied only if its argument fixes that
parameter.}

\note{ \begin{itemize}
 \item
 There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and juxtaposition
 disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have arrow types
 to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference, which
 requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
 \end{itemize}
}

== Specification/basic/expressions/reductions.tex:12-125

\section{Summations and Other Reduction Expressions}
\seclabel{reduction-expr}

\begin{Grammar}
\emph{FlowExpr} &::=&
\emph{Accumulator} \option{\emph{StaticArgs}}
\options{\texttt[ \emph{GeneratorClauseList} \texttt]} \emph{Expr} \\

\emph{Accumulator} &::=& $\sum$ $|$ $\prod$ $|$ \KWD{BIG} (\emph{Encloser} $|$ \emph{Op})
\end{Grammar}

A \emph{reduction expression} begins with a big operator such as
$\sum$ or $\prod$ followed by an optional static arguments and
an optional generator clause list (described in
\secref{generators}), followed by a body expression.
\revision{revival-reductions}{The desugaring of a reduction is directed by
type in this specification: a sum is desugared with the reduction for the type
\VAR{N} of the expression (\secref{desugaring-generators}).
Neither implementation directs it by type yet.
When no argument of the big operator fixes the element type and the bound of
its static parameter mentions the static parameter itself, as the bounds of
$\sum$, $\prod$ and \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\OPR{MIN}} do, the interpreter leaves
that parameter open (\secref{static-arg-inference}), and the reduction runs on
the types of its elements, except that an empty one takes the identity of
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the expression (row~645 of the
revival's gap ledger); the compiled type checker, when it checks the libraries
this specification describes, takes the bound of the big operator's static
parameter, which is not the element type, or, where the reduction's type at
that bound does not fit the reduction's expected type, that expected type
(\secref{static-arg-inference}): a bound such as \TYP{Number} gives the
reduction that type where it has no expected type, and a bound that mentions
the static parameter itself gives no instance that applies, so that the
reduction is refused (row~425).
Until the compiled type checker directs the desugaring by type, a reduction
with a generator clause list whose element type no argument fixes writes its
static argument in a program that both implementations are to run, as the
team's own tests do, as in
\EXP{\sum\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket [j \gets 0\#i]\: f(j)};
a reduction without a generator clause list, such as \EXP{\sum a}, needs none.
Until the compiled path is built on those libraries, it compiles against a
smaller library of its own, whose big operators $\sum$ and
\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\OPR{MAX}} take no static argument and range over
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} only; there the clause form runs without its static
argument, and a written static argument is refused.
The normative text is unchanged.}
There is no explicit relationship between \EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} and
\emph{Op}.  Instead, a reduction expression corresponds to a call to the
\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\emph{Op}} operator, which has the following header:
%% opr BIG Op[\T\](g:(Reduction[\R0\],T->R0)->R0):R
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{opr} \mathord{\OPR{BIG}}\: \emph{Op}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket(g\COLONOP(\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket,T\rightarrow{}R_{0})\rightarrow{}R_{0})\COLONOP{}R\)
\end{Fortress}
Here \VAR{R} is the result type of the operator, and \VAR{g} corresponds to
the method %generate[\R0\]
\EXP{\VAR{generate}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket}
of the trait %Generator[\T\]
\EXP{\TYP{Generator}\llbracket{}T\rrbracket}:
it is a function that takes a reduction (of type %Reduction[\R0\]
\EXP{\TYP{Reduction}\llbracket{}R_{0}\rrbracket})
and a body (of type \EXP{T\rightarrow{}R_{0}})
and returns a value of type \EXP{R_{0}} by running body on each
generated element and combining them using the reduction.
When a generator clause
list is provided, generator clauses produce values and bind the values to the
identifiers that are used in the subexpression.  Each iteration of the
body expression is assumed to be evaluated in a separate implicit
thread as described in \secref{generators}.  The resulting values are
combined together using \emph{Op}
\label{redexpr-redvar}
as with reduction variables (see \secref{reduction-vars}).
The value of a reduction expression is this combined value.
When no generator clause list is provided, the body is taken to be an
object of type \TYP{Generator} and the elements it generates are
combined.  Thus, the reduction expression \EXP{\sum a} is equivalent
to \EXP{\sum\limits_{x\leftarrow{}a}\mskip 4mu plus 4mu{x}}.

A reduction expression with a generator list:
%% \sum [v_1 \gets g_1, v_2 \gets g_2, \ldots] e
\begin{Fortress}
\(\sum [v_{\mathrm{1}} \gets g_{\mathrm{1}}, v_{\mathrm{2}} \gets g_{\mathrm{2}}, \ldots] e\)
\end{Fortress}
is equivalent to the following code:
%do
%  var result: ZZ32 = 0
%  for v1 <- g1, v2 <- g2, \ldots do
%    result += e
%  end
%  result
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{do}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{var}\:\VAR{result}\COLON \mathbb{Z}32 = 0\)\\
\(  \KWD{for}\:v_{1} \leftarrow g_{1}, v_{2} \leftarrow g_{2}, \ldots \KWD{do}\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \VAR{result} \mathrel{+}= e\)\-\\\poptabs
\(  \KWD{end}\)\\
\(  \VAR{result}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
where \VAR{result} is a fresh variable.
%
A reduction expression without a generator clause list:
%% \sum g
\begin{Fortress}
\(\sum g\)
\end{Fortress}
is equivalent to the following:
%\sum [x \gets g] x
\begin{Fortress}
\(\sum [x \gets g] x\)
\end{Fortress}
Note that reduction expressions without generator clause lists can be used to
conveniently sum any aggregate expression (described in
\secref{aggregate-expr}), since every aggregate expression
is a generator.

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1004-1078

\subsection{Reductions whose element type nothing fixes}
\seclabel{revival-reductions}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{reduction-expr}.
\item[Change] One box after the first sentence says that neither implementation
directs the desugaring of a reduction by type yet, so a reduction with a
generator clause list whose element type no argument fixes writes its static
argument; and that until the compiled path is built on the libraries this
specification describes, it compiles against a smaller library of its own,
whose big operators take no static argument and range over \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}
only, so that there the clause form runs without its static argument and a
written one is refused. The normative text is unchanged.
The box said at first that ``the interpreter, and the compiled type checker
when it checks the libraries this specification describes, each take
\TYP{BottomType} for it, and the reduction then accepts no element''; it now
says that the interpreter does, and that the compiled type checker takes the
bound of the big operator's static parameter, which gives the reduction the
type of a bound such as \TYP{Number} and no instance that applies where the
bound mentions the static parameter itself.
A revision of the interpreter of 9~October 2026 changes the box once more.
It said that ``When no argument of the big operator fixes the element type, the
interpreter takes \TYP{BottomType} for it, and the reduction then accepts no
element''; it now says that where the bound of the big operator's static
parameter mentions the static parameter itself the interpreter leaves that
parameter open and the reduction runs on the types of its elements, an empty
one taking the identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that until the compiled
type checker directs the desugaring by type a program that both implementations
are to run writes the static argument.
\item[Rationale] The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that the library's
\OPR{SUM} and \OPR{PROD} become generic reductions over the library's algebra,
each joined with its element type's own operator and taking that type's
identity, and that such a clause form writes its static argument, as the team's
own tests do.
Until 9~October 2026 the interpreter took \TYP{BottomType} for the static
parameter of a big operator that no argument fixes (row~424 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The revival decided on 8~October 2026 that the interpreter leaves open a type
parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself and that nothing at a
call fixes (\secref{revival-inference}): having no static types, the
interpreter cannot take the type \VAR{N} of the expression, and an open
parameter refuses no element where \TYP{BottomType} refused every one, so that
the reduction runs on the types of its elements, as the desugaring by type
would run it.
Reversing that revision takes one block out of the interpreter's
instantiation of a call and returns such a parameter to \TYP{BottomType}; the
specification's examples that write no static argument for such a reduction
would stop again at their first element, and refusing the call, as the compiled
type checker does, would stop them too.
The compiled type checker, when it checks the libraries this specification
describes, took \TYP{BottomType} too until it was revised to the rule of
\secref{static-arg-inference} for a type parameter that nothing at a call
fixes; it now takes the parameter's bound, which is not the element type, or,
since 14~October 2026, where the reduction's type at that bound does not fit the
reduction's expected type, that expected type, the big operator being a call
written as an argument of another call (\secref{revival-expected-contexts})
(row~425).
The compiled path's own library declares $\sum$ and
\EXP{\OPR{BIG}\:\OPR{MAX}} for \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} alone, with no static
parameter (\nolinkurl{Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi}, lines 180--184), and
refuses \EXP{\sum\llbracket\mathbb{Z}32\rrbracket [j \gets 0\#4]\: j}
(\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-numbers/probes/skeptic/SkSumClauseTyped.t1.txt}).
\item[Effect] None beyond the box: the forms without a generator clause list need
no static argument.
Since 9~October 2026, under the interpreter, a reduction with a generator clause
list whose element type nothing fixes, over a big operator whose bound mentions
its static parameter, runs where it stopped at its first element, the
specification's examples of that form among them; an empty one gives the
identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the expression (row~645
of the revival's gap ledger), and the library's set reductions \EXP{\bigcup}
and \EXP{\bigcap} still stop at their first element (row~662).
The compiled type checker still refuses that form (row~425).
\item[Original text] Unchanged.
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

== Specification/appendices/changes.tex:1666-2044

\subsection{The inference of a call's static arguments}
\seclabel{revival-inference}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \chapref{type-inference}; \secref{ranges};
\secref{basic-integers}; \secref{revival-ranges}; \secref{revival-notrevised}.
\item[Change] \chapref{type-inference}, which held a heading and two draft
notes, states how the static arguments of a call that does not write them are
inferred, for type parameters and for \KWD{nat} and \KWD{int} parameters.
The declaration is chosen first, as \secref{resolving-coercion} chooses it, a
declaration with static parameters being applicable to a call if some instance
of it within its bounds is, and compared on the parameter types it declares.
Its static arguments are then inferred: a type, \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
parameter that a parameter type mentions inside another type is fixed by the
argument, and a type parameter that the return type mentions inside another
type by the expected type; a type parameter that
is the whole type of parameters takes the narrowest type that their arguments
are substitutable for, which for number arguments is the narrowest type into
which every one of them converts, and otherwise, since 29~September 2026, its
bound (below); every
argument is admitted by substitutability, the coercions the instance needs are
inserted statically, and the converted call dispatches by subtyping.
A call written by tight juxtaposition, as a method invocation or as an operator
application, has an expected type in the contexts the chapter lists, a variable
or field declaration and an assignment to a variable among them, and is
inferred again without it when its result then converts.
A numeral whose conversions tie is read as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value; any other tie among
declarations applicable only with coercion is a static error.
The chapter lists what it does not yet describe, the static arguments of a
\KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim}, \KWD{unit} or operator parameter among them, keeps the
second of the two draft notes, and has three boxes: on the Working Draft, the
bound it assumes and the passages it leaves to the revision of the overloading
chapters; on the interpreter; and on a type parameter that only the return
type mentions and on the \KWD{bool} parameters that neither implementation
infers.
The ranges section says that a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
component converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as an integer numeral does, with a
box.
The box in \secref{basic-integers} says that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into by the rule of
\chapref{type-inference}.
\secref{revival-notrevised} says that the rule is written and names the passages
the chapter leaves unrevised, and it and the effect of \secref{revival-ranges}
say that the question of a \KWD{nat} parameter in a range is settled.
On 29~September 2026 one sentence of the rule changed.
Of a type parameter that is the whole type of parameters, where no narrowest
candidate exists and the rule for numerals does not settle the tie, the

(\secref{internal-types}), if its bounds permit that, and none of those

its declared bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and what the expected type
requires of the declared return type, none of those arguments converted, with
a box.
With the revision of the overloading chapters (\secref{revival-overloading}),
the first box points to this entry's list of the cases in which the compiled
type checker departs from the chapter and no longer names the passages that revision revised, and the box
on the interpreter says to which type the interpreter binds such a type
parameter.
A later revision adds an item to the rule: a type parameter that neither an
argument nor the expected type fixes, such as one that only the return type
mentions, as its whole type, likewise takes the intersection of its upper
bounds, and inference never instantiates a static parameter at
\TYP{BottomType}, with an example and a box.
The list of what the chapter does not yet describe named instead ``a static
parameter that neither an argument nor the expected type fixes, such as a type
parameter that only the return type mentions, as its whole type, or the element
type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine'', and left open
``whether inference may give such a parameter \TYP{BottomType}''; it now names
a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that nothing fixes, and the element type of
a reduction that only its generator clauses determine, to which the rule gives
the bound of the big operator's static parameter.
The box after the list said that the compiled type checker binds such a type
parameter to \TYP{BottomType}, except that it refuses a call with no expected
type when the parameter is declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}}, and that
``whether inference may do so is the team's question, kept in the draft note
below''; it now says that the checker follows the rule, what the compiled path's
bound \TYP{Object} makes of it, what reaches a reduction's big operator and what
the interpreter does, and that the rule answers the third item of the team's
draft note, which the chapter keeps.
A later revision of the interpreter changes both boxes on it.
The box in \secref{static-arg-inference} said that, where no argument's type is
the narrowest, the interpreter ``binds a type parameter that is the whole type
of parameters to the narrowest named common supertype of the arguments'
run-time types that the bounds permit'', the bound only where the bound is that
supertype; it now says that the interpreter gives such a type parameter its
bound, \TYP{Any} if it has none, and does the same where the arguments that fix
a type parameter inside other types have several minimal common supertypes,
except a type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter and one
declared with several bounds that the interpreter cannot meet, which it binds as
before to the narrowest named common supertype of the arguments' run-time
types, a call that fixes one of the second kind failing where there is none;
that when it chooses among declarations it passes over a declaration with
static parameters whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes in
favour of another applicable without coercion; and, until 3~October 2026, that
it instantiates at \TYP{BottomType} a type parameter that an argument bounds
only from above.
The box after the list said that ``The interpreter erases a type parameter that
nothing at a call fixes, of a function, to \TYP{BottomType}''; it now says that
the interpreter instantiates such a type parameter at its bound, and one whose
bound mentions other static parameters at that bound with their instances,
except a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions, which it instantiates at the arguments' type, and
names the type parameters it still erases: one declared with several bounds
that it cannot meet, one whose bound mentions the type parameter itself, a big
operator's that a reduction or a comprehension does not write, and one that
only the result of a function expression without a declared return type
fixes.
A revision of the interpreter of 3~October 2026 changes the box in
\secref{static-arg-inference} once more.
It said that the interpreter ``instantiates at \TYP{BottomType} a type
parameter that an argument bounds only from above, as a function argument
bounds the type parameter of its parameter type''; it now says that the
interpreter instantiates such a type parameter at the intersection of the upper
bounds that its declared bound and the arguments place on it, with two
examples, and still at \TYP{BottomType} one whose bound mentions a static
parameter or that is declared with several bounds that it cannot meet, and
that a call whose arguments place on such a type parameter two upper bounds
that it cannot meet fails.
A revision of the interpreter of 9~October 2026 changes the box after the list
once more.
It said that the interpreter ``still erases to \TYP{BottomType} a type
parameter whose bound mentions the type parameter itself, as the big operators
$\sum$ and $\prod$ declare theirs, and the static parameters of a big operator
that a reduction or a comprehension invokes without its static arguments''; it
now says that the interpreter leaves open a type parameter whose bound mentions
the type parameter itself and that nothing at a call fixes, admitting every
value where it checks a value against that type, what that gives a reduction
whose element type nothing fixes, and that it still erases the other static
parameters of such a big operator.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A.
The revival decided on 26~September 2026 that a generic call over two different
integer types infers the narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule
written into this chapter; on 27~September 2026 that the compiled type checker
infers static arguments with coercion and keeps the expected type at a call
written as \EXP{f(x)}, with a retry without it so that a coercion of the result
still applies, and that the chapter is written with it; and on 28~September
2026 that a coercion makes a call possible and never changes which declaration
runs when one is applicable without it, the declaration chosen being then
instantiated by that rule, that a numeral whose conversions tie is read as a
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, and that a \KWD{nat} parameter used as a value converts to
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} as a numeral does.
\chapref{multiple-dispatch}, \secref{idn-ref} and \secref{dotted-method-calls}
said that static arguments are inferred as \chapref{type-inference} describes,
and it described nothing; once the compiled type checker infers them by a rule
the text does not state, the text and the implementation disagree, so the
chapter states the rule the checker was built to, and the effect below lists
where the checker departs from it.
The bound in place of the union is the rule by which the dispatcher of the type
group's paper of 2019 instantiates a type parameter that the arguments do not
fix, the intersection of its upper bounds, never \TYP{BottomType}; the team
had assumed the union of the lower bounds, of which the authors write ``we were
unable to complete the proofs of correctness'' (Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu,
``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with Variance'', POPL 2019,
Section~5.4).
The paper gives no algorithm for static inference and asks of it only that it
never instantiate at \TYP{BottomType}; its one example of a static call is
typed at the union of its arguments' types.
The revival decided on 29~September 2026 to take the paper's rule for static
inference as well, which the paper allows and does not require.
The same rule gives a type parameter that neither an argument nor the expected
type fixes the intersection of its upper bounds: the paper's solving step
``never instantiates method type parameters with Bottom'' (Section~5.2), which
answers the question the Working Draft's own note asks, whether type inference
may infer \TYP{BottomType} for a static parameter.
The reasoning for that item, and for the order in which the compiled type
checker tries a call, is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-instance-bound/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The revival's decision of 29~September 2026 provided that the interpreter
follow the same rule where it instantiates a declaration, from the run-time
types of the arguments; it has no static return type to add to the bound.
It departs from the rule for the type parameters that the two boxes name,
four kinds by decision and the others as defects.
Until 9~October 2026, by decision, a type parameter whose bound mentions the
type parameter itself kept \TYP{BottomType}: it has no bound to take before its
own instance is known, the paper's calculus admits no type parameter of a
method in an upper bound (p.~11:11), and the revival had not decided that case.
The revival decided on 8~October 2026 that the interpreter leaves such a type
parameter open where nothing at a call fixes it: it does not instantiate it,
and it admits every value where it checks a value against that type.
An open type parameter is no instance: the rule that inference never
instantiates a static parameter at \TYP{BottomType} keeps a call from an
instance that admits no value, and an open parameter refuses none.
The reasoning is in \nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/p1-judgement.md} in the
revival's repository.
By decision, a big operator's static parameter whose bound does not mention it,
that a reduction or a comprehension does not write, keeps \TYP{BottomType}: it
is the element type of the reduction, which this chapter does not yet
describe, and from \TYP{BottomType} the interpreter's
library builds a comprehension's collection at the type of its elements, where
from the bound it would build it at the bound.
By decision, a type parameter that only the bound of a type parameter that the
arguments fix mentions takes the arguments' type: the interpreter has no
expected type to fix it, and the library's operator that appends two covariant
collections builds its result at such a type parameter, which at its bound
would be \TYP{Any}.
By decision, a lone type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter,
itself or another, keeps the narrowest named common supertype of the arguments
rather than its bound: the interpreter cannot evaluate such a bound before the
instances are known, and keeping the candidates it had leaves unchanged the
case of a type parameter whose bound mentions itself and that the arguments
fix, which the revival has not yet decided.
As defects, each gated by an expected failure of the revival's tests, the
interpreter erases to \TYP{BottomType} a type parameter declared with several
bounds that it cannot meet, having no intersection type, and a type parameter
that only the result of a function expression without a declared return type
fixes, since it gives that result the type \TYP{BottomType}.
Until 3~October 2026 it also erased a type parameter that an argument bounds
only from above, taking the lower end of the interval that the arguments give
the type parameter; it now takes the upper end, the intersection of the upper
bounds that the rule gives, except, as defects gated by expected failures, for
a type parameter whose bound mentions a static parameter, which it cannot
evaluate before the instances are known, and one declared with several bounds
that it cannot meet.
The reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-walk-instance/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
The order, a declaration chosen and then instantiated, is that of
\secref{resolving-coercion}, read on the parameter types that declarations
declare, as the type group's paper of 2011 reads a declaration with static
parameters: it ``is applicable to a type if and only if at least one of its
instances is'' (\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 396--397, in the
revival's repository).
The numeral's default is what the interpreter did before this change, giving
a numeral the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, \library\ declaring their numeral type
below \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}; the compiled path, whose library declares its
numeral type beside \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and excluding it, took one of the
declarations that a numeral left tied, and not always the same one (row~391 of
the revival's gap ledger).
It is also the Java programming language's type for an integer literal.
The compiled type checker gives a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter used as a
value the type of a numeral, and the interpreter makes it a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
so an \KWD{int} parameter is read as a \KWD{nat} parameter is; on the Java
Virtual Machine the length and the indices of an array are 32-bit integers.
The team's later Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives the coercion relation,
the coercion of a generic type and the valid instantiations of a quantified
type (\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
938--947, 393--400 and 771--789, in the revival's repository) and never uses
the word ``infer''; the type group's paper leaves the run-time inference of the
static arguments of a dispatched declaration ``beyond the scope of this paper''
(\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 118--129).
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-spec-inference/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] A generic call over two different integer types, or over a number
type and a numeral, need not write its static argument, and the interim rule
of the effect of \secref{revival-numbers} ends.
A declared type fixes a type parameter that the return type of a call written
as \EXP{f(x)} mentions inside another type, and a call whose result the
declared type converts is accepted as before.
Where the conversions of a numeral tie, the \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} declaration or
instance is taken; where another argument's conversions tie, the call is a
static error.
A \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter may be a component of a range, as in the
specification's own examples.
The overloading chapters compare declarations on the parameter types they
declare and infer static arguments after the selection, and \secref{type-param}
gives a type parameter without an \KWD{extends} clause the bound \TYP{Any}
(\secref{revival-overloading}, \secref{revival-bound}).
A type parameter that nothing at a call fixes is instantiated at its bound
under the expected type and never at \TYP{BottomType}: a call whose compiled
run failed loading an instance over \TYP{BottomType}, or failed verification
where the call's result was carried as one, now runs; a call with no expected
type whose type parameter is declared \EXP{\KWD{extends} \TYP{Any}} is
accepted; and a call where the bound and the expected type have no common
subtype, such as a type parameter bounded by \TYP{Object} where \TYP{()} is
expected, is a static error unless the result of the instance at the bound
converts to the expected type.
The compiled type checker departed from the chapter in five cases, each gated
by an expected failure of its tests, until it was revised with the item above:
the expected type could let a declaration applicable only with coercion be
chosen over a declaration with static parameters that is applicable without it
(row~508 of the revival's gap ledger); a call that the rule instantiates at the
bound, with another argument converted, was refused (row~515); a type parameter
declared without an \KWD{extends} clause, which has no narrowest candidate, was
instantiated at the union of the arguments' types where the chapter gives
\TYP{Any} (row~516); an argument that is an instance at a union, which only the
checker's own union made, was refused where it fixes a type parameter
(row~518); and an argument whose static type is an intersection, which the
typing of a call between two traits with \KWD{comprises} clauses gives
(\secref{revival-meet}), fixed a type parameter at one of its conjuncts
(row~541).
It now follows the chapter in each, trying a call by subtyping without the
expected type first and keeping that attempt when its result converts to the
expected type, and the five tests are plain tests of the rule.
The compiled path's run time does not yet load an instance at an intersection
type (row~559), which the rule gives by two routes: an argument whose static
type is an intersection, as in the last of them, and a type parameter that
nothing at a call fixes whose declared bound and expected type are two traits
that meet at their intersection.
A program that the compiled path ran before this revision, at one conjunct of
such an intersection or at \TYP{BottomType}, now dies loading that instance.
A written bound, such as \TYP{Number}, is taken by both implementations where
the chapter gives it.

Under the interpreter, a type parameter that nothing at a call fixes runs at its
bound where it ran at \TYP{BottomType}, and a type parameter with no narrowest
candidate at its bound where it ran at the arguments' narrowest named common
supertype, except the type parameters that the boxes on the interpreter name;
a call whose arguments have several minimal common supertypes runs where it
stopped the interpreter, unless they fix a type parameter declared with several
bounds that the interpreter cannot meet or one whose bound mentions the type
parameter itself.
Since 3~October 2026, under the interpreter, a type parameter that an argument
bounds only from above runs at the intersection of its upper bounds where it ran at
\TYP{BottomType}, except the type parameters that the box in
\secref{static-arg-inference} names; a call whose arguments place on such a
type parameter two upper bounds that the interpreter cannot meet, as functions
of two traits neither of which extends the other do, still fails with an error
of unification, as it failed before (row~616 of the revival's gap ledger).
Since 9~October 2026, under the interpreter, a type parameter whose bound
mentions the type parameter itself and that nothing at a call fixes is left
open where it was instantiated at \TYP{BottomType}, so that a reduction whose
element type nothing fixes runs on the types of its elements where it stopped
at its first element (\secref{revival-reductions}); an empty such reduction
takes the identity of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} whatever the type of the expression
(row~645), and the library's set reductions \EXP{\bigcup} and
\EXP{\bigcap}, whose reductions take sets of the open type, still stop
(row~662).
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/inference.tex},
lines 12--27, which held after the chapter's heading two draft notes:
\begin{quote}
This chapter will include the Fortress static type inference mechanism.
\end{quote}
and the note that the chapter keeps:
\begin{quote}
\begin{itemize}
\item There seems to be a circular dependency between inference and
juxtaposition disambiguation -- you have to know if the subexpressions have
arrow types to disambiguate, but you can't do that without using inference,
which requires knowing how the variable of unknown type is used.
\item Type Inference (Dan's email titled ``Comments on a first reading of the
spec'' on 06/05/07)
\item Do we want to forbid such cases where type inference infers
\TYP{BottomType}s for static parameters?
\end{itemize}
\end{quote}
The other passages this change revises are the revival's own text of 27 and
28~September 2026, not the Working Draft's.
The ranges section said, in
\nolinkurl{Specification/basic/expressions/ranges.tex}, lines 46--48, before
this revision:
\begin{quote}
An integer numeral converts to \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} (\secref{literals}), and
it is a static error if a component of an explicit range has an integer type
other than \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}.
\end{quote}
The box in \secref{basic-integers} ended, in
\nolinkurl{Specification/basic-lib/basic-integers.tex}, lines 90--94:
\begin{quote}
A generic call over two different integer types is to infer the
narrowest type that both coerce into, by a rule to be written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation; until then such a
call writes its static argument, as in
\EXP{f\llbracket\mathbb{Z}64\rrbracket(a, b)}.
\end{quote}
The effect of \secref{revival-ranges} ended:
\begin{quote}
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter may be a component of a range is not settled
(\secref{revival-notrevised}).
\end{quote}
and \secref{revival-notrevised} said:
\begin{quote}
The rule by which a generic call over two different integer types
infers the narrowest type that both coerce into is to be written into
\chapref{type-inference} together with its implementation
(\secref{revival-numbers}).
\end{quote}
and
\begin{quote}
Whether a \KWD{nat} parameter, which may appear wherever a variable of type
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} can (\secref{natparams}), may be a component of a range
is not settled (\secref{revival-ranges}); the static ranges of
\secref{ranges} and the examples whose ranges a \KWD{nat} parameter bounds are

\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

component InferUnfixedBoundWalk
export Executable

(* A type parameter that no argument fixes, its bound not mentioning it, takes its declared bound, Any if it has none, never BottomType (ledger row 424). *)

object BoxU[\T\]() end

thr[\T\](): T = throw ForbiddenException(CallerViolation)

mkN[\T extends Number\](): BoxU[\T\] = BoxU[\T\]()
mkU[\T\](): BoxU[\T\] = BoxU[\T\]()
none[\T\](xs: T...): BoxU[\T\] = BoxU[\T\]()
mkB[\T extends Number, U extends BoxU[\T\]\](): BoxU[\U\] = BoxU[\U\]()

witness[\T extends Number\](): String = typecase thr[\T\] of
    () -> ZZ32 => "ZZ32"
    () -> Number => "Number"
    else => "other"
  end

kindU(x: Any): String = typecase x of
    BoxU[\BoxU[\Number\]\] => "BoxU[BoxU[Number]]"
    BoxU[\Number\] => "BoxU[Number]"
    BoxU[\Any\] => "BoxU[Any]"
    else => "other"
  end

run(): () = do
    assert(kindU(mkN()), "BoxU[Number]", "a type parameter bounded by Number that nothing at the call fixes takes its bound Number (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(kindU(mkU()), "BoxU[Any]", "a type parameter without a bound that nothing at the call fixes takes Any (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(witness(), "Number", "the () -> T witness of a parameter bounded by Number that nothing fixes takes the Number clause, not the first (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(kindU(none()), "BoxU[Any]", "a varargs parameter given no argument leaves its type parameter to its bound Any (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    assert(kindU(mkB()), "BoxU[BoxU[Number]]", "a type parameter bounded by BoxU[T] that nothing fixes takes that bound at the instance of T, which takes its bound Number (inference.tex, section \"The Static Arguments of a Call\")")
    println("PASS")
  end

end

341:PRETYPECHECKDESUGAR produces code that must itself be type-checked: comprehensions and big operators become `__generate`/`__bigOperator`/`__bigOperator2` calls against the library's reduction objects, generator lists become `exp.loop(fn x => body, gs)` chains, and generalized `if`/`while` become `__cond`/`__whileCond` (`PreTypeCheckDesugaringVisitor.java:142-165,245,301,333-335`).
423:`MainWrapper.main` loads the named class through `InstantiatingClassloader.ONLY` and invokes its no-argument `main` (`runtimeSystem/MainWrapper.java:19,60-67`); program arguments are stashed in a static field rather than passed (`:65`).
425:`InstantiatingClassloader.loadClass` (`runtimeSystem/InstantiatingClassloader.java:178`) is where compiled Fortress stops being ordinary bytecode: a class name is examined for markers, and depending on what it finds the loader *generates* the class rather than reading it.
427:It generates: tuple and arrow RTTI classes, closure classes, arrow interfaces and their abstract and wrapped forms, tuple types, union types, and — the general case — an instantiation of a generic template, by reading the template's bytes and rewriting them with ASM through `Instantiater` and an `InstantiationMap` (`:210-290,376-406`, `runtimeSystem/Instantiater.java:17-54`).
429:Instantiation renames; it does not change representation. `Instantiater.visit` substitutes type names in the class name, superclass and interfaces (`Instantiater.java:40-54`).
455:There is no way for a Fortress program to be called *from* Java other than by loading the generated classes through `InstantiatingClassloader`, which is what `MainWrapper` does.
